material_type: Fine-grained polycrystalline quartz-rich material; often classified as aventurine quartz or aventurine quartzite
composition: Primarily SiO2 with mica inclusions, commonly chromium-bearing fuchsite
crystal_system: Quartz grains are trigonal; finished material is a polycrystalline aggregate
formation: Metamorphic quartz-rich rock containing reflective mineral inclusions
common_localities: India, Brazil, Russia, Austria, Tanzania, Canada, United States
treatments: May be oiled, dyed, or polymer impregnated; treatment is not universal
imitations: Aventurine glass, green glass, jade, and other green ornamental materials
care: Mild soap, lukewarm water, soft cloth; avoid harsh chemicals and prolonged soaking when treatment is unknown
source_note: Technical framing corrected from the initial Claude draft; retain source verification in MD research notes

formation: Natural citrine forms in igneous and metamorphic settings and is relatively rare. Most commercial citrine is heat-treated amethyst or smoky quartz that turns yellow to orange when heated to approximately 470 to 560 degrees Celsius.
color_range: Pale yellow to deep amber; heat-treated material ranges to orange and brownish-orange
common_localities: Brazil (primary commercial source), France, Madagascar, Russia, Scotland, Spain, United States (California, Colorado, North Carolina)
treatments: Most commercial citrine is heat-treated amethyst or smoky quartz. Natural pale yellow citrine exists but is uncommon. Deeply uniform orange-red material (trade name Madeira Citrine) is almost always treated. Color from heat treatment is generally stable.
imitations: Heat-treated amethyst (widely sold as citrine), yellow topaz, yellow glass, synthetic quartz
care: Stable under normal conditions; prolonged direct sunlight may fade color in treated material. Clean with mild soap and water; avoid harsh chemicals.
alternate_names: Madeira Citrine (deep orange-red trade name); Merchant's Stone (popular metaphysical name); historically called False Topaz or Topaz Quartz
source_note: Book of Stones (A+): silicon dioxide, hexagonal/trigonal crystal system, hardness 7, iron-derived color, localities include Brazil, Russia, France, Scotland, Africa, Madagascar. B-tier source adds Spain and US localities. Treatment distinction and heat temperature range from mineralogical reference.

material_type: Transparent to translucent gypsum (true selenite). Note: most commercial selenite wands and plates are satin spar, the fibrous chatoyant variety of gypsum — distinct in structure but sold under the same public name.
formation: Evaporite deposits formed by evaporation of mineral-rich water; also occurs in hydrothermal veins, cave environments, and as a secondary mineral in clay beds.
transparency: Transparent to translucent (true selenite); fibrous satin spar is translucent with silky chatoyance
color_range: Colorless to white; also pale grey, beige, and peach
color_cause: Essentially colorless when pure; trace minerals and inclusions cause tinting
common_localities: Mexico (primary source for clear selenite), Morocco, Algeria, Brazil, Australia, Poland, United States, United Kingdom
treatments: Occasionally oiled; rarely dyed. Satin spar pieces are cut and polished from fibrous gypsum material; this is mechanical shaping, not chemical treatment.
imitations: Clear calcite (Iceland spar), acrylic or plastic pieces sold as selenite
care: Extremely soft (hardness 2); scratches very easily. Water soluble with prolonged contact — avoid soaking or extended water cleansing. Do not store with harder minerals. Handle gently.
alternate_names: Satin Spar (fibrous gypsum variety most commonly sold as selenite); Desert Rose (rosette-forming gypsum variety); Alabaster (massive granular gypsum); Gypsum (mineral species name)
source_note: Book of Stones (A+): hydrous calcium sulfate mineral, monoclinic crystal system, hardness 2, form of gypsum called Selenite when clear and well-formed, best clear specimens from Mexico. Satin spar distinction and additional localities from mineralogical reference.

material_type: Complex borosilicate mineral; schorl variety of the tourmaline group
crystal_system: Trigonal (rhombohedral); Book of Stones and many popular sources describe it as hexagonal — a historical grouping that included trigonal
formation: Igneous environments, primarily granites and pegmatites; also metamorphic settings and hydrothermal veins.
common_localities: Brazil, United States (California, Maine), Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Madagascar, Russia, China, various African localities
treatments: Generally untreated. Sometimes oiled to enhance polish. Tumbled and polished commercial pieces are common.
imitations: Black obsidian, black kyanite, black glass, jet, morion (black quartz)
care: Durable for most uses at hardness 6 to 7.5. Clean with mild soap and water; avoid harsh chemicals.
source_note: Book of Stones (A+): complex aluminum borosilicate, hexagonal crystal system, hardness 6 to 7.5, opaque black, found in Brazil, China, Pakistan, Africa, USA. B-tier source adds Afghanistan, Madagascar, Russia, Sri Lanka, California, Maine. Schorl is the correct mineralogical species name. Crystal system noted as trigonal (rhombohedral) per current mineralogical classification.
